nameStory: This little moth gets its name from its favorite food plant, the Ailanthus tree (also called Tree of Heaven), where its caterpillars create silky webs as they feed. The 'webworm' part refers to these protective silk shelters the larvae spin around leaves and branches. It's like having your own personal dining tent!
description: The Ailanthus Webworm Moth is a small, strikingly colorful moth that's easy to mistake for something else entirely. When resting, its bright orange body with metallic blue spots and white-spotted dark wings make it look more like a beetle or true bug than a moth. In flight, it mimics a wasp with its quick, erratic movements and colorful pattern. These little moths are only about half an inch long but pack a visual punch with their tropical-looking colors.

idTips.label: Wing pattern
idTips.description: Dark forewings covered with neat rows of bright white spots that shimmer slightly in sunlight, creating an almost polka-dotted appearance

idTips.label: Body coloration
idTips.description: Brilliant orange-red body decorated with iridescent blue-green spots that catch the light like tiny jewels

idTips.label: Resting posture
idTips.description: Holds wings roof-like over its body when at rest, looking surprisingly beetle-like rather than moth-like

idTips.label: Flight behavior
idTips.description: Flies during the day with quick, jerky movements that mimic wasps, often hovering briefly at flowers

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Tiny moth with wingspan barely reaching half an inch, small enough to sit comfortably on your fingernail

habitat: Look for these moths anywhere Ailanthus trees (Tree of Heaven) grow, which in New England means disturbed areas, vacant lots, roadsides, and forest edges. They're particularly common in urban and suburban areas where these invasive trees thrive. You'll also find them around the original host plant, Paradise Tree, in warmer microclimates.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, becoming active on warm, sunny days. Look for them visiting small flowers or resting on tree trunks.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with multiple generations. Adults are most visible during hot, sunny days, often seen around Ailanthus trees where females lay eggs.
seasonality.fall: Late-season adults may still be active on warm days. Caterpillars create more noticeable webbing on host trees as they prepare for winter.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off with frost, but pupae overwinter in protected spots like bark crevices or leaf litter around host trees.

funFact: This tropical moth has become an unlikely hero in the fight against invasive species — its caterpillars can completely defoliate Ailanthus trees, helping to weaken these aggressive invaders that crowd out native New England plants!
confusionNotes: Often mistaken for beetles, true bugs, or wasps rather than moths due to its bright colors and daytime activity. Remember: if it has feathery or thread-like antennae and holds its wings tent-like over its body, it's the moth — beetles have clubbed antennae and hard wing covers.
contextualKnowledge: This moth is actually a recent arrival to New England, having expanded north from the tropics as it adapted to feed on the invasive Ailanthus tree. It's a perfect example of how species ranges can shift when new food sources become available.
compareHints: As the only Atteva species in New England, compare it to other small, colorful day-flying moths like the Virginia Ctenucha or Spotted Oleander Moth. However, none of these have the distinctive combination of bright orange body with blue spots and white-spotted black wings that makes the Ailanthus Webworm so unmistakable.
